newsitem.title: TURKEY: Kinkel says Turkey has place in European family.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel says Turkey has place in European family.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel traded barbs with Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan but assured Ankara on Wednesday that it still had a place in the European family.
"Turkey belongs to Europe. The Turkish train remains on the main track, it will not be put on the side track," Kinkel told a news conference during a visit to Ankara.

However, he listed Turkey's human rights problem, economic troubles, an armed Kurdish rebellion and quarrels with European Union member Greece as serious obstacles to eventual Turkish membership in the EU.
Erbakan and Kinkel later held talks. Speaking to journalists after the meeting, Kinkel said a row over comments made by Erbakan before the visit had not soured relations between the two countries.

"Naturally there is no bad atmosphere between Germany and Turkey...where there are problems it is to be hoped that they are discussed and that is what happened," Kinkel told reporters after meeting Erbakan.
Kinkel's conciliatory line followed a public dispute with Erbakan in which the two exchanged accusations over Turkey's trade ties to Europe.
"No European will have to bow their head to Turkey in shame," Kinkel told reporters earlier on Wednesday.
He was close to calling off the trip because of media reports quoting Erbakan as urging Kinkel to repent in a dispute over a trade deal between Turkey and the European Union.
Turkey and some leading EU countries have been on a collision course since Ankara threatened in January to veto NATO's planned expansion if it were not given guarantees of EU membership.

Erbakan urged Germany not to reject Turkey's European ambitions. "I hope that in this decisive year 1997 our German friends and other friendly countries will not make any wrong decisions," Erbakan told reporters before talks with Kinkel.
Leading European Christian Democrats, angered by the Turkish threat to block NATO, said at a meeting this month that Turkey was unfit to join the EU, partly because of its Moslem culture.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who attended the meeting, took the brunt of Turkish criticism of the comments. Kinkel and other EU foreign ministers have since distanced themselves from the Christian Democrats.
Turkey has been an associate member of the EU since 1963 and says it is unjust that other countries, including former east European adversaries, are likely to get into the EU before it.
Kinkel arrived in Turkey two hours late on Tuesday night after he delayed his departure from Rome to check comments by Erbakan, secular Turkey's first Islamist prime minister.

Erbakan told MPs of his Welfare Party on Tuesday that Turkey should be treated with more respect internationally. He blamed Europe for what he said were losses because of a customs accord with the EU that went into effect at the start of 1996.
"There will be a $5 billion loss for Turkey because it has entered the customs union...After they have done this they will bow their heads when they talk with Turkey," Erbakan said.
EU exports to Turkey have surged under the accord, while Turkish exports to the bloc have changed little.
Erbakan has promised a more independent foreign policy since he came to power last June.

"It will be very interesting to meet with him (Kinkel). Now nobody can give Turkey the 'do this, do that' treatment... The respect and treatment which the new world leader Turkey deserves will be realised," he said.

Millions of dollars in EU aid to Ankara under the customs union have been blocked by Turkey's traditional foe Greece over disputes in Cyprus and the Aegean and by EU states concerned about Turkey's human rights record.
